common_name: Captain Cook Croton (Narrow Strap-Leaf Hedge Croton)
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Captain Cook croton carries long, narrow, strap-shaped leaves in dark green with bold yellow to orange midribs and veining, giving a finer-textured, more upright look than broad-leaved selections like Petra or Mammy. Its tidy, columnar growth habit and tolerance of regular shearing make it a long-time favorite as a clipped hedge, screen, or foundation planting in South Florida and Hawaii landscapes. Bright light brings out the strongest vein color; water when the top inch of soil dries and protect from any frost.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. King Kalakaua bears solid red single blooms on a vigorous, upright shrub, and is better known among hibiscus breeders as a long-used hybridizing parent than as a modern bedding selection, having contributed its color and form to many later crosses. Grow it the same as other tropical hibiscus: prune hard in early spring to renew wood and maximize bloom, and feed with a slow-release fertilizer every four to six weeks through the growing season. Each flower lasts only a single day before the next flush opens.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Mystic Pink produces soft pink blooms shading toward white at the petal base, a gentler pastel presentation than the bold reds and oranges of older Hawaiian cultivars, and has been used by breeders as a parent for newer pastel-flowered hybrids. Culture is the same as other tropical hibiscus: prune hard in early spring to renew growth and maximize flowering, and feed with a slow-release fertilizer every four to six weeks through the growing season. Flowers are day-blooming and typically last only a single day.

This Canary Island endemic, often treated as a subspecies of Viburnum tinus, is a bold evergreen shrub with thick, deeply veined leathery leaves and rounded clusters of small white flowers in late winter and spring. The flowers give way to showy fruit that passes through red before ripening to glossy blue-black. Once established in a mild, frost-free garden it tolerates considerable drought and poor soil, making it a durable structural shrub for Mediterranean-climate plantings. Give it an open, sunny to lightly shaded spot and prune lightly after flowering to keep its dense habit tidy.

Native to the laurel-forest margins and ravines of the Canary Islands and Madeira, this evergreen spurge forms a rounded dome of whorled, blue-green lance-shaped leaves on bare stems. In spring it produces dense, rounded clusters of brownish-red flowers with a surprisingly strong honey scent that draws in bees and other pollinators. It thrives on neglect once rooted in, wanting sharp drainage and a sunny, sheltered site, and like other spurges exudes an irritant milky sap that calls for gloves when pruning. It has become a popular structural plant in dry Mediterranean-climate borders and coastal gardens.

This fast-growing shrub from the laurel-forest margins of the Canary Islands carries narrow evergreen leaves and a long season of bright yellow, five-petaled flowers from summer into autumn. It builds a loose, woody framework quickly, which makes it useful for fast screening or informal hedging in mild coastal gardens, but it also means it benefits from an occasional hard prune to prevent legginess. Because it seeds and naturalizes readily in warm coastal climates outside its native range, it is best sited where self-sown seedlings can be managed or removed. Give it full sun and lean, free-draining soil to keep growth sturdy rather than sprawling.

Native to the shaded understory and forest margins of the Canary Islands and Madeira, this unusual scrambling relative of butcher's broom replaces true leaves with flattened, leaf-like stems called cladodes that twine and clamber over neighboring vegetation. Tiny flowers are borne directly on the edges of these cladodes and are followed by orange berries on female plants grown near a male. It wants the dappled light, shelter, and steady moisture of a woodland-edge setting and cannot tolerate hard frost, so in cooler regions it is grown as a conservatory or sheltered courtyard curiosity. Its strange architecture has made it a favorite of collectors specializing in unusual evergreen foliage plants.

A relict fern of the Azorean, Madeiran, and Canarian laurisilva, with a smaller outlying population in northern Iberia, this species forms a broad, spreading crown of soft, finely divided fronds from a creeping, fibrous rootstock. It favors the constant humidity, deep shade, and sheltered ravines typical of cloud-forest understory, and it cannot tolerate drying wind or prolonged freezing. In mild, humid gardens such as those found in coastal Cornwall it has been grown successfully as a dramatic shade-garden specimen. Steady moisture and leaf-litter mulch that mimics its native forest floor are key to keeping it healthy.

Amau is a Hawaiian endemic tree fern whose new fronds emerge a striking wine-red before maturing to deep green, eventually building a short, shaggy trunk-like caudex with age. Give it humus-rich, consistently moist but not waterlogged soil in dappled or partial shade, sheltered from drying wind; it is more tolerant of brighter light and disturbed, mineral volcanic soils than most tropical tree ferns, which is why it colonizes lava flows and forest gaps in its native range. It resents hard frost and is best grown outdoors only in essentially frost-free climates, or as a large container specimen elsewhere. Historically significant in Hawaiian culture for dye and fiber, it also makes a dramatic textural anchor for a shaded tropical border.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources (CTAHR)

directions: This small South American epiphyte creeps along bark or a mounting slab on a thin, wiry rhizome, sending up short, leathery, oval fronds that resemble a string of blueberry leaves rather than a typical lacy fern frond. Grow it mounted on wood or in a shallow pan of chunky, fast-draining epiphyte mix in bright shade with steady humidity, misting or watering whenever the mount begins to dry rather than keeping it constantly wet. It spreads slowly into a low mat or trailing curtain, making it a good miniature companion for an orchid or epiphyte display rather than a standalone specimen. Protect it from any frost and from strong direct sun, which scorches its thin fronds.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
